accuracy.evidence: Checked against NC England KS3 Physics Waves (colours and frequencies of light, white light and prisms, absorption and diffuse reflection); spectrum order and wavelengths (red about 700 nm, violet about 400 nm) and the fact that glass refracts violet most; Newton (1672) for recombining with a second prism. The lab and adult text say plainly that red, green and blue parts are the school model, and every shirt, banana and filter result follows that model (red shirt in blue light black, white shirt in green light green, yellow banana under a red filter red, cyan plus blue filter blue, red plus green filters no light).

misconceptions.evidence: Predictions target the prism adding colour, red bending most, coloured light mixing like paint (red shirt in blue light predicted purple) and filters adding colour; band feedback names an upside-down order or a one-place slip; challenge and step feedback cover an object keeping its colour, white versus black, filters adding up, and same-colour filter stacks.

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is an optics bench for this topic: a ray box and prism throwing a seven-band spectrum with a frequency arrow, a drop zone for an upside-down second prism that rejoins the colours to white, a lamp lighting shirts and a banana in coloured light, two-slot filter stacks with a preset cyan filter, and a lamp filter that sets an object's seen colour. It only works for white light and colour.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner acts first and the result explains: wrong band names get the order rule, tapping red as most bent shows it is nearest the straight-on path, the second prism turns the spectrum white (so the glass adds nothing), wrong shirt colours are answered with what the object can reflect, and wrong filter stacks show the colour that actually reaches the screen before the reply.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options: the glass adds the colours (the rejoin step disproves it), red bends most (the spectrum shows red least bent), purple for a red shirt in blue light (the scene shows black), and a red filter adds red (the filter stacks show filters only subtract).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with its own slip (flip, order, near, adds, paint, reflectall, keeps, white, addfilter, second, blackwhite, blacklight, yellowblue, yellowgreen); for example Yellow light for red then green filters gets the reply Filters only take light away.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and defines refract, frequency, reflect, absorb and filter where they first appear, passing the kid readability limit in validate_lessons; adult text names the curriculum and the model in plain language.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (the spectrum, dispersion and rejoining, coloured objects, filters); adult paragraphs give the curriculum link, the physics and the model, the common mistakes and what the lab does, with no template text.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes: the dark optics bench fills the width, the seven bands stay readable at 340 px, colour tiles sit in two columns, filter tiles in one, shirt and filter labels fit the bench and nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a tray button (colour names then Band 1-7 from the top, the band that bent most, Put the second prism in, each shirt colour, each filter); filters carry colour names as well as swatches; the canvas aria-label is updated with each reply; walk.cjs reports axe clean in both themes on desktop and phone with every Show me task completing.
